newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan justice minister breaks taboo on executions.
newsitem.headline: Japan justice minister breaks taboo on executions.

text.p: Japanese Justice Minister Isao Matsuura broke a long taboo on Tuesday by publicly revealing that he signed orders to hang three convicted murderers.
"I did sign (the orders) for the executions," Matsuura told a news conference.
Matsuura was the first Japanese minister to formally acknowledge ordering executions.
Human rights activists had said three death-row inmates were executed at the Tokyo Detention House last Friday.
The activists said two of those executed had killed bar hostesses and robbed them in Tokyo in 1978.
In a separate case, the third man killed three members of his family including his father-in-law and mother-in-law for refusing to lend him money in 1983.
The Justice Ministry's long-standing policy is to make no public announcement or comment out of deference for the privacy of the families of those executed.
The ministry also refuses to discuss why particular convicts are selected for execution. Nor are outside witnesses allowed to observe the hangings.

Neither the condemned man nor his family has any advance warning of an execution. The Justice Ministry says the prisoner is not told to avoid upsetting him. The ministry will not answer questions about how hangings are scheduled.
Once one takes place, human rights campaigners and activist lawyers say, it can be days, even months, before the news becomes public.
"(Previous) justice ministers had said they know nothing (about executions). But if I sign the orders, I can't say I don't know," Justice Minister Matsuura said.
"I will change the policy," he added.
Japan has hanged more than 580 criminals since 1945. Anti-hanging campaigners believe there are more than 50 convicts on death row at present.
Japan had stopped executions in November 1989, raising a glimmer of hope among anti-hanging campaigners that it would let the practice wither.
But the government resumed executions in March 1993. Since then 21 people, including the three last Friday, have been hanged, according to human rights activists.
